workEn: Popol Vuh (The Council Book of the K'iche' Maya)
title: Catepuch xe bixanic, xe zuanic
titleEn: Popol Vuh — The grandmother laughs; the monkeys go to the forest; the field that clears itself
part: The grandmother laughs; the monkeys go to the forest; the field that clears itself
source: Popol Vuh, “The grandmother laughs; the monkeys go to the forest; the field that clears itself”, from the only surviving copy: the K'iche' text in the hand of Fray Francisco Ximénez, written at Chichicastenango c. 1701–1703 (Newberry Library, Chicago, Ayer MS 1515, fols. 19r–20v, left-hand column), read from the Library of Congress / World Digital Library images; public domain. The text is the manuscript's own spelling, including the colonial letters ꜩ (tz), ꜯ (tz'), ꜭ (k'), ꜭh (ch') and ꜫ (q'), v for u and w, z for s, h for j, and c/qu for both k and q. Where Ximénez's cursive makes these letters hard to tell apart, the reading of Brasseur de Bourbourg's edition (Paris, 1861), made from the same manuscript, was used as a check. Word division, punctuation, capitals and quotation marks are editorial. The ꜩ→tz button shows every word in the modern K'iche' alphabet; there an ejective or glottal stop the scribe left unmarked is supplied where the word is certain, and a word whose modern form is uncertain is simply respelled. Pronunciation: modern K'iche' values for the modern spelling, an admitted convention. No prepared audio yet. All translations were made fresh from the K'iche' for Lectorium.

sentences.t: Catepuch xe bixanic, xe zuanic, xe cohomanic, ta vcamic ri qui zu, qui cohom; ta xcube puch ri catit cuꜭ.
sentences.l: Then-also they sang, they played-the-flute, they drummed, when its-taking the their flute, their drum; then she-sat-down also the their-grandmother with-them.
sentences.i: Then they sang, they played the flute and beat the drum, taking up their flutes and their drums; and their grandmother sat down with them.
sentences.n: Three verbs of one shape: xe 'they' + a verb in -an + -ic. bixan 'sing' is bix 'song' + -an; zuan 'play the flute' is zu 'flute' + -an (014); cohoman 'drum' is cohom 'drum' + -an. -an makes a verb of action with no object, and -ic closes the clause. Brasseur's note: the cohom is a drum of hollow wood with a skin over one end only, which the Spaniards called atabal. Ximénez writes cohom with plain c, and Brasseur writes gohom (= ꜫ). The modern word is q'ojom 'drum, music', so the toggle restores the q' (q'ojom, q'ojomanik). vcamic 'the taking': v- 'its' + cam 'take' + -ic (Brasseur u qamic). The toggle gives uk'amik with his q, as 006's xquicam; the 'take' verb is still an open question (QUESTIONS 007/3). xcube 'she sat down': x- + cub 'sit' (toggle xkub'e). ri catit cuꜭ 'their grandmother with them' (MS cug, read ꜭ). In the narrative catit is c- 'their' + atit (toggle katit); in the twins' speech it is 'our grandmother' (qatit). Ximénez abbreviates catit and atit throughout (cah̃t, ah̃t), and they are written out here.

sentences.t: Ta xe zuanic, xe ziquix pa zu, pa bix, ta xu binaah ri Hunahpu Coy vbi zu.
sentences.l: Then they played-the-flute, they-were-called in flute, in song, then it-named-it the Hunahpu Coy its-name flute.
sentences.i: As they played, the elder brothers were summoned with flute and with song, and the tune was given its name, Hunahpu Coy.
sentences.n: xe ziquix 'they were called': ziquih 'call' (modern sik'ij) + the passive -ix. It is the elder brothers who are called, as the next line shows. pa zu, pa bix 'with flute, with song', a couplet that comes back in ¶3. xu binaah 'it named it': x- + u- 'he, it' (singular) + binaah 'give a name' (bi 'name'); the doer is not stated (toggle b'inaaj by the letters). Hunahpu Coy vbi zu 'Hunahpu Coy, the name of the flute (tune)': coy 'monkey' has plain c here, as at the end of 014, where the house word is ꜭoy. The toggle gives K'oy, and the name means 'Hunahpu Monkey'.

sentences.t: Ta xe oc cu vloc ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, que xahouic ta xe vlic.
sentences.l: Then they entered then hither the Hunbatz, Hunchouen, they dancing when they arrived-here.
sentences.i: Then Hunbatz and Hunchouen came in, dancing as they came.
sentences.n: xe oc … vloc 'they came in': oc 'enter' with vloc 'hither, this way'. que xahouic 'dancing': que 'they' (k- ongoing + e) + xahou 'dance' + -ic. The modern word is xajoj 'dance'; the toggle respells the letters (xajowik). xe vlic 'they arrived here'.

sentences.t: Catepuch ta xmucun ri atit iꜩel qui vach, xril atit, ta xꜩeenic; maui xu cui vꜩe atit.
sentences.l: Then-also when she-looked the old-woman, ugly their face, she-saw-it the-old-woman, then she-laughed; not she-held-back her-laughter the-old-woman.
sentences.i: Then the old woman looked, and when she saw their ugly faces she laughed; the old woman could not hold back her laughter.
sentences.n: xmucun 'she looked' (mucun 'look'). iꜩel qui vach 'ugly their faces': iꜩel 'evil, bad', here 'ugly'. xꜩeenic 'she laughed': x- completive + ꜩeen 'laugh' (ꜩe 'laughter' + -n) + -ic; here the x is the plain completive, not the ix 'you (pl.)' Brasseur sees in 014's mi xꜩeenic. maui xu cui vꜩe 'she did not hold back her laughter': cui is read as the verb of 014's cuya 'endure, bear', here 'hold in' (inferred). The MS has xucui with i, and Brasseur prints x-u cuy; the toggle gives kuy. vꜩe 'her laughter': v- + ꜩe (toggle utze'). atit means 'old woman' as well as 'grandmother'.

sentences.t: Xa cu huzu xebec, maui xil chi qui vach.
sentences.l: Only then at-once they-went, not was-seen any-more their face.
sentences.i: At once they were gone, and their faces were seen no more.
sentences.n: huzu 'at once' (toggle jusuk, as earlier parts). xebec 'they went': x- + e 'they' + be 'go' + -c. maui xil chi qui vach 'their faces were not seen any more': xil has no ergative prefix (she saw it is xril, as in ¶2's xril atit), so it is the passive of il 'see', as xil rumal catit in ¶19. chi is taken as chic 'any more' with its c shared with the next word, as the glossary's chi and the earlier parts have it (toggle chik).

sentences.t: “Eia, catit! Xebe pa quechelah.
sentences.l: “Look, our-grandmother! They-went into forest.
sentences.i: “See, grandmother! They have gone into the forest.
sentences.n: Eia is an exclamation, not otherwise known; Brasseur prints Eya! and translates 'Voyez-vous!' (inferred; toggle Eya, the i a y). Doubtful reading: the MS has eia cahic, and the last word lacks its final stroke. It is read catit with Brasseur (k'atit). In the twins' mouths catit is 'our grandmother' (toggle qatit). quechelah 'forest', as in 013 and 014.

sentences.t: Naquipa chi bano, ix catit? Xa cahmul xchi ca tiho, xa oxmul chic.
sentences.l: What you(?)-do-it, you our-grandmother? Only four-times shall we try-it, only three-times now.
sentences.i: What have you done (?), grandmother? We may try only four times, and now there are only three left.
sentences.n: Naquipa 'what'. chi bano has no completive x-. chi is taken as ch- + i- 'you (pl.)', the plural of respect to the grandmother, as in ix catit (inferred); Brasseur has 'Qu'avez-vous fait'. cahmul 'four times' and oxmul 'three times': cah 'four', ox 'three' + mul 'times' (toggle kajmul, oxmul). xchi ca tiho 'we shall try it': xchi- future + ca 'we' + tih 'try' + -o. xa oxmul chic 'only three now', since one of the four has been used.

sentences.t: Xque ca ziquih pa zu, pa bix; qui chi cuyu iꜩe. Catiha china,” xeꜭha chic Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: Them-shall we call in flute, in song; (qui) let-you hold-back your-laughter. We-try(?)-it again(?) now(?),” they-said again Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: We shall call them with the flute and with song; hold back your laughter. Let us try again (?),” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Xque ca ziquih 'we shall call them': xque is the future x- + que 'them' (the object), and ca 'we' is the doer (toggle xke qa sik'ij). pa zu, pa bix 'with flute, with song', the couplet of ¶1. qui chi cuyu iꜩe 'hold back your laughter' (Brasseur 'retenez votre rire'). chi is taken as ch- + i- 'you (pl.)' (inferred), cuyu is the cui of ¶2 with -u, and iꜩe is i- 'your (pl.)' + ꜩe 'laughter' (toggle itze'). The y of cuyu is clear here; ¶6 writes cuiu. qui is not clear (toggle ki by the letters). Catiha china is a doubtful reading: the MS has cathha / china across a line break, with the t written like h, and it is read Catiha. Brasseur divides ca üha chi na. The English takes it as ca 'we' + tih 'try' + -a, with chi(c) 'again' and na 'now' (a guess; toggle Katija china by the letters).

sentences.t: Cate xe zuan chic; ta xe oc chi vloc, que xahou chic. Xe vl chic chi vnicahal vvaha.
sentences.l: Then they played-the-flute again; then they entered (chi) hither, they dancing again. They came-here again to its-middle (vvaha).
sentences.i: Then they played the flute again, and in they came once more, dancing. They came right into the middle of the house (?).
sentences.n: zuan and xahou have no -ic here because a word (chic) follows; -ic comes only at the end of a clause. chi before vloc is not clear (toggle chi). vnicahal 'its middle': v- + nicah 'middle, half' + -al (toggle unik'ajal, as nik'aj in 008 and 009). vvaha: Brasseur prints u va-ha and translates 'jusqu'au milieu de la salle'. ha is 'house' (012), but the va is not clear, and 'of the house' is inferred (toggle uwaja by the letters).

sentences.t: Xavi cu ꜫuz ca qui bano, xavi ca qui tacchih ri catit chi ꜩe; libahchi xꜩeen chiri catit.
sentences.l: Just then ꜫuz(?) they-do-it, just they urge(?) the their-grandmother to laughter; in-a-moment she-laughed there their-grandmother.
sentences.i: They made such sport (?), they so stirred (?) their grandmother to laughter, that in a moment she burst out laughing.
sentences.n: Xavi … xavi 'just so … just so': two lines in parallel. Xavi cu ꜫuz is the weakest reading in the part. The MS has xa | vi ququz, two q/g-shaped letters each followed by u. It is printed with Brasseur's xavi cu guz: the first letter read c, the second ꜫ. ꜫuz is not otherwise known. 'Sport, delight' follows Brasseur's 'donnant tant de plaisir' (a guess; toggle q'us). ca qui bano 'they do it': ca ongoing + qui 'they' (toggle ka ki). tacchih is written tac chih, as two words on the page, and is joined here with Brasseur's takchyih. It is not otherwise known; 'stir, urge' follows his 'excitant si bien sa gaîté' (a guess). chi ꜩe 'to laughter'. libahchi 'in a moment' (as 010; Brasseur 'bientôt'). xꜩeen 'she laughed', without -ic before chiri.

sentences.t: Quiꜩih ꜩeebal qui vach ri coy, chi xiri ri e xe qui pam, chi chitila he puch vchi qui ꜭux, ta xe oc vloc; are cut qui chu ꜩeeh atit.
sentences.l: Truly laughable their face the monkey, (chi) xiri(?) the they under their belly, (chi) wagging(?) tail also, its-mouth their heart, when they entered hither; this then (qui) she-laughed-at-it the-old-woman.
sentences.i: Truly their monkey faces were a thing to laugh at, and the bulge (?) under their bellies, the wagging (?) of their tails and their chests (?), as they came in; and so the old woman laughed at them.
sentences.n: ꜩeebal 'a thing to laugh at': ꜩe 'laughter' + -bal, the ending of means and place (toggle tze'b'al). ri coy 'the monkeys', with plain c as in ¶1 (toggle k'oy). xiri is not otherwise known; 'bulk, swelling' follows Brasseur's 'l'ampleur de leur bas-ventre' (a guess). xe qui pam 'under their bellies' (as 014's xe i pam; toggle xe'). chi chitila he is a doubtful reading: the MS has chichihta he, with tall strokes after chichi. Brasseur's chi chitila is taken, and 'wagging' follows his 'frétillement de leurs queues' (a guess). he is 'tail' (014; toggle je'). vchi qui ꜭux 'the mouth of their hearts' is taken as the chest or the pit of the stomach (Brasseur 'le plat de leur estomac'; inferred; MS quigux, read ꜭ). chu ꜩeeh 'she laughed at it': ꜩe + -h makes the verb transitive (toggle tze'j). chu is ch- + u- 'she', without the sense 'let'. qui before it is not clear: 'them' would be e, not qui, before a transitive verb. Brasseur's 'il y avait bien de quoi faire rire' suggests qui 'truly', as in qui ꜩih (a guess; toggle ki by the letters).

sentences.t: Cate xebe chic pa tac huiub.
sentences.l: Then they-went again into (tac) mountains.
sentences.i: Then they went off again into the mountains.
sentences.n: pa tac huiub 'into the mountains': tac marks things many and scattered. huiub is huyub with i for y; the image has i here, where Brasseur prints huyub (toggle juyub').

sentences.t: “Naquipa xchi ca bano, ix catit? Xere chi va roxmul chic xchi ca tiho,” xꜭha ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: “What shall we do-it, you our-grandmother? Only (chi) this its-third-time now shall we try-it,” he-said the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: “What shall we do, grandmother? This will be only the third time we try,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: xchi ca bano is a doubtful reading: the first letter is q-shaped and is read x. Brasseur has chi ka bano, with no x. roxmul 'its third time': r- 'its' + ox 'three' + mul 'times'. Xere chi va 'only this'. xꜭha is singular for two speakers, as Ximénez writes it.

sentences.t: Xe zuan chic; xe vl chic que xahauic. Xa cu chu cuiu ca vꜩe ri catit.
sentences.l: They played-the-flute again; they came-here again, they dancing. Only then she held-back (ca) her-laughter the their-grandmother.
sentences.i: They played the flute again, and again they came in dancing. This time their grandmother held back her laughter.
sentences.n: xahauic is xahouic with a for o (toggle xajawik by the letters). chu cuiu ca vꜩe 'she held in her laughter': chu (ch- + u- 'she', without the sense 'let'), cuiu the cuyu of ¶3, written with i (MS chucuiuca; Brasseur ch'u cuyu ca). ca is a particle that is not clear. Brasseur adds 'momentanément': she held it in for a while.

sentences.t: Xe acan cu vloc chu catanah ꜩac; caꜫruxruh vchi tac qui vach, muꜩumac qui chi, chi quimal qui chi, qui vach, macama chi qui hoꜫih chique.
sentences.l: They climbed then hither at-its catanah(?) wall(?); red-glaring(?) its-mouths (tac) their face, pushed-out(?) their mouth, (chi) twisted(?) their mouth, their face, macama(?) (chi) their grimacing(?) to-them.
sentences.i: Then they climbed up onto the top (?) of the house, their eyes glaring red (?), their mouths pushed out (?), their mouths and their faces twisted (?), pulling faces (?) of every kind (?) at one another.
sentences.n: Xe acan … vloc 'they climbed up' (acan 'climb'; toggle aq'an, as earlier parts). chu catanah ꜩac: Brasseur 'à la terrasse de la maison'. catanah is not otherwise known, and ꜩac is taken as 'wall, building' (inferred; toggle katanaj tzaq by the letters). A list of the monkeys' faces follows, each part with qui 'their'. Most of its words are known only from Brasseur's French and are guesses. caꜫruxruh has the tresillo (Brasseur ca-kruxruh) and is taken as 'glaring red', perhaps built on caꜫ 'red' (010; inferred). vchi tac qui vach 'the openings of their faces' are their eyes (Brasseur 'leurs grands yeux rouges'). muꜩumac qui chi 'their mouths pushed out' (his 'museau allongé'). chi quimal 'twisted'. macama is a doubtful reading: there is an ink blot on the second a, and Brasseur prints makamo ('de toute sorte'). qui hoꜫih 'their grimaces': the MS has hoquih, and q + u is read ꜫ with Brasseur's hogih. chique 'to them', here to one another (inferred).

sentences.t: Ta xril chicut ri atit, cate xpocolih chi vꜩe ri catit. Ma chi cu xil chi qui vach rumal vꜩebal atit.
sentences.l: Then she-saw-it again-then the old-woman, then she-burst(?) at her-laughter the their-grandmother. Not (chi) then was-seen any-more their face because-of her-laughing the-old-woman.
sentences.i: But when the old woman looked at them again, their grandmother burst out laughing; and because of the old woman's laughter their faces were seen no more.
sentences.n: xpocolih 'she burst out' is not otherwise known; it follows Brasseur's 'elle éclata de rire' (inferred; toggle xpokolij). vꜩebal 'her laughing': ꜩe + -bal, written with one e here and with two in ¶4's ꜩeebal (toggle utze'b'al in both). Ma chi … xil chi 'no more were seen', as ¶2's maui xil chi: xil, without r-, is the passive (Brasseur 'on ne revit plus'). The second chi is chic 'any more' with its c shared (toggle chik, as ¶2); the first is left as written (toggle chi). rumal 'because of'.

sentences.t: “Xere vi cua, ix catit, xque ca pixabah vbic chu cahmul cut.”
sentences.l: “Only-this (vi) cua(?), you our-grandmother, them-shall we summon(?) thither at-its fourth-time then.”
sentences.i: “Just this once more (?), grandmother: we shall summon them a fourth time.”
sentences.n: Xere vi 'just this'. cua is not otherwise known; Brasseur has 'Cette fois seulement' (toggle kua by the letters). xque ca pixabah 'we shall summon them' is built like xque ca ziquih in ¶3: future x- + que 'them' + ca 'we'. pixabah is 'charge, give an order' (pixab 'counsel'). With vbic 'thither' it is taken as 'call out', after Brasseur's 'nous les appellerons hors (des bois)' (inferred). chu cahmul 'at the fourth time': chi + v- 'its' + cahmul. No tag follows; the speakers are the twins.

sentences.t: Xe zuax chic; macu xe vl chic chu cahmul; huzu xebec pa quechelah.
sentences.l: They-were-fluted again; but-not they came-here again at-its fourth-time; at-once they-went into forest.
sentences.i: Once more the flute was played to call them; but the fourth time they did not come back, and went straight off into the forest.
sentences.n: xe zuax: zu 'flute' + the passive -x, 'they were fluted to', called by the flute (inferred; Brasseur 'Ils furent appelés une fois de plus au son de la flûte'; toggle suax). macu 'but not' (ma + cu; toggle mak'u, as 014).

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cut chire catit: “Mi cu xca tiho, ix catit; mi nabe xe vlic, mi pu xca tih chic qui ziquixic.
sentences.l: They-said then to-her their-grandmother: “Just-now then we-tried-it, you our-grandmother; just-now first they came-here, just-now also we-tried again their-being-called.
sentences.i: Then they said to their grandmother: “We have tried, grandmother. At first they came, and then we tried once more to call them.
sentences.n: chire catit 'to their grandmother' in the narrative (toggle katit), ix catit 'our grandmother' in the speech (toggle qatit). mi before a completive verb marks what has just happened: mi xca tiho 'we have just tried it'. mi … mi pu … 'just now … and just now …', two lines in parallel. qui ziquixic 'their being called': ziquih 'call' + passive -ix + -ic (toggle sik'ixik, as 013's vziquixic).

sentences.t: Mi xbizon cut; oh ꜭolic, oh iviy, xa chilo coh ri ca chuch, ix catit.
sentences.l: Do-not you(?)-grieve then; we are-here, we your-grandchildren, only let-you(?)-look-on-it us the our mother, you our-grandmother.
sentences.i: Do not grieve: we are here, we, your grandchildren; only look on us (?), our mother, grandmother.
sentences.n: Mi xbizon 'do not grieve', as in 010 and 014's mi xbizonic, here without -ic before cut. Brasseur divides it M'yx bizon, mi + ix 'you (pl.)' (inferred). oh ꜭolic, oh iviy 'we are here, we your grandchildren', a couplet (MS ohgolic, read ꜭ with Brasseur's qolic). ꜭolic is 'being there'. iviy is a doubtful expansion: the MS writes ivy with a mark above, read as an abbreviation of the i of viy 'grandchild' (Brasseur y'viy). It is iv- 'your (pl.)', the form of i- before a vowel (modern iw-), + iy 'grandchild' (toggle iwiy); ix viy in ¶12 has v- 'my' + iy. xa chilo coh ri ca chuch is taken as chilo, ch- + i- 'you (pl.)', the plural of respect of ¶3's chi bano, + il 'see' + -o, with coh 'us' as the one seen: 'only look on us, our mother' (a guess). coh is k- + oh, the absolutive 'we, us', and cannot be the doer of a transitive verb, which would take ca 'we'. Brasseur divides ch'ilo koh and translates 'nous vous regarderons comme notre mère', with the twins as the doers; the letters do not support his person. ri ca chuch 'our mother' (toggle qa).

sentences.t: Que nabax ri caꜩ, ta chuxoc mi xe ꜭobic, mi pu xe binahic Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, que vꜭhaxic,” xeꜭha ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: They are-remembered(?) the our-elder-brothers, so let-it-be: just-now they ꜭobic(?), just-now also they were-named Hunbatz, Hunchouen, they are-called,” they-said the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: Our elder brothers are remembered (?), and so let it be: they have been known (?), they have been named Hunbatz and Hunchouen, as they are called,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Que nabax: que 'they' (ongoing) + nabax 'be remembered' (uncertain). This is 002's nabax, paired there with ziquixoc 'be called upon'; Brasseur has 'en mémoire de nos aînés'. ri caꜩ 'our elder brothers' (toggle qatz, as in 014's speeches). ta chuxoc 'so let it be': ch- optative + ux 'become' + -oc. xe ꜭobic is uncertain. The MS has xegobic with the g-shaped letter, printed ꜭ by the shape rule; Brasseur reads x-e cobie with plain c and does not help. The meaning is not known: 'they were known' is a guess from its partner xe binahic 'they were named' (toggle k'ob'ik by the letters). mi … mi pu … is again a couplet. xe binahic 'they were named' (bi 'name', as binaah in ¶1). que vꜭhaxic 'as they are called' (toggle ke uch'axik).

sentences.t: Xe ziquix cut rumal ri ahzu, ahbix, ri oher vinac; are puch chu ziquih ri ahzib, ahcot oher.
sentences.l: They-were-called-upon then by the flute-players, singers, the old people; this also they-call-on the painters, carvers of-old.
sentences.i: They were called upon by the flute players and singers, the people of old; and the painters and carvers of old called upon them too.
sentences.n: Xe ziquix 'they were called upon': ziquih 'call' + passive -ix (toggle sik'ix). Hunbatz and Hunchouen become the patrons of the crafts that were theirs in 014. The flute players and singers are ahzu, ahbix, and the painters and carvers ahzib, ahcot: ah- 'one who' + zu 'flute', bix 'song', zib 'paint, write', cot 'carve'. ahzib has plain z, as 014's ahzibab (toggle ajsib'). chu ziquih 'they call on them' is active, with chu (u-, singular) where the doers are plural. Brasseur: 'c'étaient eux qu'invoquaient également les peintres et les sculpteurs'.

sentences.t: Xe chicopiric, e coy xe vxic, rumal xax qui nimarizah quib, xqui yoc ri qui chac.
sentences.l: They-became-animals, they monkey they-became, because truly they made-great themselves, they-mistreated(?) the their younger-brothers.
sentences.i: They became animals, they became monkeys, because they had made themselves great and mistreated their younger brothers.
sentences.n: Xe chicopiric 'they became animals': chicop 'animal' + -ir 'become' + -ic, a verb made from a noun (toggle chikopirik). e coy xe vxic 'monkeys they became': vx 'become' (toggle k'oy). xax 'truly', as in 001, 008 and 009; since qui nimarizah has no x- of its own, xax may also be xa 'only' + the verb's x-, written on xa (inferred). qui nimarizah quib 'they made themselves great', the boasting of Vucub Caquix in 004–005. xqui yoc 'they mistreated' follows Brasseur's 'qu'ils maltraitaient leurs frères' (inferred). He writes yog, which suggests yoq' 'abuse', but the toggle respells the letters (yok), as 014's vyoc. Both yoc and chac have plain c (Brasseur yog, chag). qui chac 'their younger brothers' (toggle chaq', as 011 and 014).

sentences.t: Quehe vi calabil chi qui ꜭux, quehe cut qui maixic ri ta xe zachic ri Hunbaꜩ, Hunchouen, e chicop xe vxic.
sentences.l: Thus (vi) the-ruin(?) at their heart, thus then their being-destroyed(?) when they were-lost the Hunbatz, Hunchouen, they animals they-became.
sentences.i: Such was the ruin (?) of their hearts, such the undoing (?) of Hunbatz and Hunchouen, when they were lost and became animals.
sentences.n: Quehe … quehe cut 'thus … thus', a couplet. calabil 'ruin' is written with plain c (Brasseur galabil, 'Ainsi fut l'anéantissement de leur raison'). It is taken from the calaba 'lay waste' of 013 and 014 (inferred; toggle kalab'il by the letters). Brasseur's note: ꜭux 'heart' here means the mind, the reason. qui maixic 'their undoing': mai 'destroy (?)', as 012's maixel, + passive -x + -ic (inferred). xe zachic 'they were lost' (zach 'be lost').

sentences.t: Are cut e ramaꜫelal co cochoch chic; xavi xere e ahzu, e ahbix nim chic xqui bano, ta xe coheic ruꜭ ratit, ruꜭ pu qui chuch.
sentences.l: This then they always(?) there-is their-home now; just so they flute-players, they singers, great things now they-did-it, when they were-there with-her his-grandmother, with-her also their mother.
sentences.i: Yet they had always lived at home (?); they were flute players and singers, and they did great things while they lived with their grandmother and their mother.
sentences.n: e ramaꜫelal is read as r- + amaꜫel 'always' (004) + -al, 'at all times' (inferred). The MS has ramaquelal, and q + u is read ꜫ with Brasseur's r'amagelal ('Or, ils étaient constamment dans leurs maisons'). co cochoch 'their home was (there)': co 'there is' (toggle k'o) + cochoch 'their home'. The MS has cocho-|ch, with a doubled c at the line join, divided co cochoch. e ahzu, e ahbix 'they were flute players, they were singers'. xe coheic 'they were there, they lived' has plain c here, where 014 wrote the g-shaped ꜭoheic (Brasseur qoheic). The word is certain, so the toggle restores the k' (k'oje'ik). ruꜭ ratit 'with their grandmother': r- 'his, her' is singular, the grandmother of each.

sentences.t: Ta xqui tiquiba chicut qui banoh, qui cutbal quib chuvach catit, chuvach pu qui chuch.
sentences.l: Then they-began again-then their work, their showing themselves before their-grandmother, before also their mother.
sentences.i: Then they began their own work, to show what they were before their grandmother and before their mother.
sentences.n: Ximénez starts a new paragraph here, and the twins take their turn. xqui tiquiba 'they began' (tiquiba 'plant, begin', as in the book's first line). qui cutbal quib 'their means of showing themselves': cut 'show' (the cutun 'appear' of 001) + -bal + quib 'themselves' (Brasseur 'pour se manifester aux yeux de leur aïeule'; toggle k'utb'al). chuvach … chuvach pu … 'before … and before …', a couplet.

sentences.t: Nabe xqui bano ri abix. “Xa coh abixic, ix catit, ix pu ca chuch,” xeꜭha.
sentences.l: First they-made-it the field. “Only we are-making-field, you our-grandmother, you also our mother,” they-said.
sentences.i: First they made a maize field. “We are going to clear a field, grandmother, and you, our mother,” they said.
sentences.n: abix 'maize field, milpa' (013). abixic is the noun made a verb, 'clearing and working a field' (Brasseur's note: the first work of civilisation). coh 'we' (ongoing). ix catit, ix pu ca chuch 'you, grandmother, and you, our mother', a couplet (toggle qatit, qa chuch).

sentences.t: “Mi xbizonic; oh ꜭolic, oh iviy, oh qui ꜫexel caꜩ,” xeꜭha cu ri Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.l: “Do-not you(?)-grieve; we are-here, we your-grandchildren, we their replacement our-elder-brothers,” they-said then the Hunahpu, Xbalanque.
sentences.i: “Do not grieve: we are here, your grandchildren; we are here in place of our elder brothers,” said Hunahpu and Xbalanque.
sentences.n: Mi xbizonic, oh ꜭolic, oh iviy as in ¶8. iviy is again the MS ivy with a mark above (toggle iwiy). qui ꜫexel caꜩ 'the replacement of our elder brothers': qui 'their' + ꜫexel, the house vꜫexel 'replacement'. The MS has quexel, and q + u is read ꜫ (toggle q'exel). caꜩ follows it, 'our elder brothers' (toggle qatz).

sentences.t: Ta xqui cam cut quicah, qui mixquina, qui xoquem; xebec ruꜭ huhun qui vvb xqui teleh. Xe el chi cochoch.
sentences.l: Then they-took then their-axe, their hoe, their xoquem(?); they-went with each their blowgun they-carried-it-on-the-shoulder. They went-out from their-home.
sentences.i: Then they took up their axes, their hoes and their digging sticks (?), and set off, each with his blowgun on his shoulder. They left their home.
sentences.n: xqui cam 'they took' (toggle k'am, as 006's xquicam, with Brasseur's q). quicah 'their axes' is written joined (Brasseur qu'icah, qui + icah) and the reader takes it as one word. icah 'axe' is the word of the next paragraphs (toggle kikaj). mixquina 'hoe' (Brasseur 'pioches'). xoquem is not otherwise known. Brasseur has 'charrues' (ploughs), which cannot be right before the Spanish came; a digging stick is a guess. ruꜭ huhun qui vvb 'each with their blowgun': huhun 'each one' (toggle wub', as after qui in 008). xqui teleh 'they carried it on the shoulder' (005). Xe el chi cochoch 'they went out from their home'.

sentences.t: Ta xqui pixab cu catit chire vyaic qui va: “Chi ticoh na ꜫih, chi be ya ca va, ix catit,” xeꜭha.
sentences.l: Then they-instructed then their-grandmother to-her its-giving their food: “When it-stands(?) (na) the-sun, let go give our food, you our-grandmother,” they-said.
sentences.i: And they told their grandmother when to bring their food: “When the sun stands overhead (?), bring us our food, grandmother,” they said.
sentences.n: xqui pixab 'they instructed': pixab 'counsel, instruction', here a verb (Brasseur 'en recommandant'). vyaic 'its giving': v- + ya 'give' + -ic. qui va 'their food': va, modern wa, 'food, the tortilla'. Chi ticoh na ꜫih: ticoh is taken from tic 'plant, set upright' (as tiquiba), 'when the sun stands up', which is noon (Brasseur 'A midi juste'; inferred). In na ꜫih the MS has quih, and q + u is read ꜫ (Brasseur gih). chi be ya ca va 'let our food be brought': chi optative, be 'go', ya 'give'. ca va 'our food' (toggle qa wa).

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala, ix viy,” xꜭha cut ri catit.
sentences.l: “Good bala, you my-grandchildren,” she-said then the their-grandmother.
sentences.i: “Very well, my grandchildren,” said their grandmother.
sentences.n: Vꜩ bala 'Very well', the house rendering. ix viy 'you, my grandchildren': v- 'my' + iy 'grandchild'. The MS writes ixvy with the same mark above as iviy, read as an abbreviation of the i (Brasseur yx viy; toggle wiy). xꜭha is singular: she said.

sentences.t: Catecut xe opon chiri que abix vi; xaqui xqui chiquiba ri mixquina pa vleu.
sentences.l: Then-then they arrived-there there they make-field (vi); simply they-thrust-it the hoe in earth.
sentences.i: Then they came to the place where they were to make their field, and simply drove the hoe into the ground.
sentences.n: que abix vi 'where they make the field': que 'they' (ongoing) + abix used as a verb, with vi pointing back to the place. xaqui 'simply, only' (Brasseur xaki; inferred). xqui chiquiba 'they drove it in' follows Brasseur's 'ils enfoncèrent la pioche dans la terre' (inferred). It is the verb of 014's ichiquiba 'cast down'.

sentences.t: Xa cu qui chi tahin ri mixquina pu vleu, ma cu qui chi tahin ri mixquina chutuquel.
sentences.l: Only then (qui) (chi) be-at-it the hoe in-the earth, not then (qui) (chi) be-at-it the hoe by-itself?
sentences.i: So the hoe set to work in the ground; and was the hoe not at work all by itself (?)?
sentences.n: Xa cu … ma cu … 'only then … not then …', two lines in parallel. tahin 'be at it, at work', the progressive tajin. qui chi before tahin is not clear (toggle by the letters). chutuquel 'by itself' has plain t in the MS (Brasseur ch'utuquel); it is chi + utuquel 'alone' (modern utukel; toggle chutukel). The English takes the second line as a question that expects 'yes' (inferred); Brasseur's version is loose here. pu vleu 'in the earth': pu is pa 'in' + v-.

sentences.t: Are curi icah xavi chi qui chiquiba chu toloc che, xavi chu cab rib che chi bec, chi lahahic chi bec ronohel che, caam; ꜫaꜫchacachoh chic chi catoh che chu ban ri xa huna icah.
sentences.l: This then-the axe just (chi) they-thrust-it at-its trunk tree, just at-its arm itself tree (chi) going, (chi) felled(?) (chi) going all tree, vine; crashing(?) now (chi) cutting tree it-did-it the only one axe.
sentences.i: And the axe, too, they drove into the trunks of the trees and into their branches; down they went, felled (?), all the trees and the vines, crashing (?) down, cut through, and a single axe did it all.
sentences.n: The axe's work is set beside the hoe's: xavi … xavi 'and also … and also'. chu toloc che 'into the trunk of the tree' (Brasseur 'dans la souche des arbres'; toloc is not otherwise known, inferred). chu cab rib che 'into the branches of the tree itself': cab 'arm, branch' has plain c (Brasseur gab; toggle q'ab', as 014's chu cab tac che). chi bec 'going'. chi lahahic 'being felled' is not otherwise known (Brasseur 'jetant par terre'; inferred). che, caam 'trees, vines', the pair for the whole forest. caam is written caã in the MS, an abbreviation (toggle k'a'm). ꜫaꜫchacachoh, with two tresillos (Brasseur cakchacachoh), is not otherwise known; 'crashing down' is a guess from its sound and his 'faisant tomber tout'. chi catoh che 'cutting trees': catoh has plain c (Brasseur gatoh). It is the ꜫatoh 'cut' of ¶18, the word is certain, and the toggle restores the q' (q'atoj). xa huna icah 'only one axe': huna, from hun 'one' (inferred).

sentences.t: Are curi mixquina ꜩaꜩ chi cupuh; maui ahilan tum quixic cu ban ri xa hun chi mixquina; maui ahilan cupuh xa chuti huyub, nima huyub ca hec.
sentences.l: This then-the hoe much (chi) clearing(?); not counted brambles(?), thorns it-does-it the only one (chi) hoe; not counted clearing(?) only small mountain, great mountain it-is-pulled-up(?).
sentences.i: And the hoe: great was its clearing. The brambles (?) and thorns that one hoe alone cleared could not be counted; there was no counting what was cleared and pulled up (?) on the small mountains and the great mountains.
sentences.n: ꜩaꜩ 'many, dense' (toggle tzatz). cupuh 'clearing, pulling up' is not otherwise known; it follows Brasseur's 'ce que la pioche arrachait' (inferred; toggle kupuj). maui ahilan … maui ahilan 'not counted … not counted', two lines in parallel (ahilan 'counted', 004). tum is printed as read; the sense 'brambles' is Brasseur's ('ronces'), a guess. Brasseur's text reads tum here and tam in ¶20, where the MS has tun with only two minims. quixic 'thorns': quix 'thorn' (014; toggle k'ix) + -ic (toggle k'ixik). xa chuti huyub, nima huyub 'the small mountains, the great mountains', the whole land (014). ca hec 'is pulled up' (Brasseur 'jeté par terre'; inferred; toggle ka jek by the letters).

sentences.t: Ta xqui pixabah cut hun chicop, Xmucur vbi; xqui tuyuba acan oc chuvi nima cutam.
sentences.l: Then they-instructed then one animal, Xmucur its-name; they-set-it up (oc) on-top great stump.
sentences.i: Then they gave their orders to a creature called Xmucur, and set it up on top of a great stump.
sentences.n: Xmucur is a dove (Brasseur 'le Pigeon-Ramier'; the modern xmukur is a wild dove; inferred), kept as a name. chicop is any creature (Brasseur's note: the animal, the beast, and by extension the savage). xqui tuyuba 'they set it' is not otherwise known (Brasseur 'l'ayant fait monter'; inferred). acan oc 'up': acan 'climb', with oc, the ending of direction after a verb of motion (toggle aq'an oq, as acan oc in 012 and 013). cutam 'stump, trunk' (Brasseur 'tronc d'arbre'; toggle kutam by the letters).

sentences.t: Xeꜭha cut Hunahpu, Xbalanque: “Xa chavil ri catit chi petic iaol ca va; huzu cat oꜫic ta petoc; catecut chi ca chap ri mixquina ruꜭ icah.”
sentences.l: They-said then Hunahpu, Xbalanque: “Only you-watch the our-grandmother (chi) coming, bringer our food; at-once you-shall cry when she-comes; then-then let we-seize-it the hoe with axe.”
sentences.i: Hunahpu and Xbalanque said: “Just watch for our grandmother coming with our food; call out as soon as she comes, and then we will take up the hoe and the axe.”
sentences.n: chavil 'watch': ch- (command) + av- 'you (one)', the form of a- before a vowel (modern aw-), + il 'see'. chi petic 'coming'. iaol ca va 'the bringer of our food': ya 'give' + -ol, an agent noun, as 009/010's yaol (MS iaol with i, Brasseur yaol; toggle yaol). cat oꜫic 'you shall cry': cat 'you (one) shall' + oꜫ 'weep, cry', the dove's call. The MS has catoquic, and q + u is read ꜫ (Brasseur c'at ogic; toggle kat oq'ik). ta petoc 'when she comes': pet 'come' + -oc. chi ca chap 'let us seize it'.

sentences.t: “Vꜩ bala,” xꜭha curi Xmucur.
sentences.l: “Good bala,” it-said then-the Xmucur.
sentences.i: “Very well,” said Xmucur.
sentences.n: Vꜩ bala 'Very well', the grandmother's answer in ¶12, now the dove's. xꜭha 'it said', singular.

sentences.t: Are cut xa vvbanic chi qui bano, mana quiꜩih abixic ta chi qui bano.
sentences.l: This then only blowgunning (chi) they-did-it, not truly field-making (ta) (chi) they-did-it.
sentences.i: But all they did was hunt with the blowgun; they did no real work on the field.
sentences.n: vvbanic 'hunting with the blowgun' (014; toggle wub'anik). mana … ta 'not': the negative ma(na) with ta after the thing denied, as with maui … ta. quiꜩih 'truly'. The same verb, chi qui bano, ends both lines.

sentences.t: Catepuch choc ri Xmucur; anim cut que petic, hun chi chapo mixquina, hun cut chi chapon ri icah.
sentences.l: Then-also it-cried(?) the Xmucur; quickly then they come, one (chi) seizes-it hoe, one then (chi) seizes the axe.
sentences.i: Then Xmucur called out, and quickly they came running: one seized the hoe, and the other seized the axe.
sentences.n: choc 'it cried' is taken as ch- + oc, the oꜫ 'cry' of the last paragraph written with plain c (Brasseur ch'og, 'le Pigeon-Ramier roucoula'; inferred). The toggle respells the letters (chok), which are the same as the glossary's chok 'enter', a different word. hun … hun cut 'one … and the other'. chapo 'seize it' has the -o of a transitive verb; chapon has -on, with the thing seized named after it.

sentences.t: Chi qui piz la qui vi; xaloc chu bacala vleu pu cab ri hun, xa quehe chu ꜩiloh vvach, queheri quiꜩih abixom.
sentences.l: (chi) they-wrapped(?) (la) their head; for-nothing(?) he-smeared(?) earth on-his hand the one, only thus he-dirtied his-face, like truly a-field-worker.
sentences.i: They wrapped up (?) their heads; and for nothing (?) one of them smeared earth on his hands and dirtied his face as well, just like a real field worker.
sentences.n: Chi qui piz la qui vi: piz and la are kept apart as Brasseur has them (piz at the end of a line, la at the start of the next). la is not clear, and 'wrap' follows his 'S'étant enveloppé la tête' (inferred). qui vi 'their heads' (vi 'head', toggle wi'). xaloc 'in vain, for nothing' comes four times in these lines. Brasseur's note explains it as xa 'only' + log 'love', 'gratuitement' (inferred); the MS has plain c (toggle xalok by the letters). chu bacala 'he smeared' (Brasseur 'se couvrit … les mains de terre'; inferred). pu cab 'on his hands' has plain c (Brasseur gab; toggle q'ab'). chu ꜩiloh vvach 'he dirtied his face': ꜩil 'dirty' (modern tz'il). Ximénez writes the plain ligature; the toggle supplies the glottal stop, as in 009's Junb'atz'. abixom 'one who has worked the field': -om marks the doer of a finished action.

sentences.t: Are curi hunchic xaloc chu puquih vvebal che pu holom, quehe viri quiꜩih ꜫatoh cheenel.
sentences.l: This then-the other for-nothing(?) he-scattered(?) its-chips tree on-his head, thus (viri) truly cutting tree-worker.
sentences.i: And the other, for nothing (?), scattered wood chips over his head, as if he had truly been cutting trees as a woodsman.
sentences.n: hunchic 'the other' (hun 'one' + chic). chu puquih 'he scattered' and vvebal che 'chips of wood' follow Brasseur's 'se remplit … la tête d'échardes de bois' (inferred). pu holom 'on his head': the MS has puholom, and Brasseur prints u holom. quehe viri: the MS has queheuiri, with Ximénez's v-shaped r, divided quehe viri (Brasseur З viri). ꜫatoh cheenel 'a cutter of trees, a woodsman': the MS has gatoh with the g-shaped letter and no u after it, so the hand could be ꜭ or ꜫ. Brasseur (gatoh) decided ꜫ, and the modern q'atoj 'cut' agrees. cheenel: che 'tree' + -nel, an agent noun (toggle che'enel). The two lines are a pair, one twin as the field worker, one as the woodsman.

sentences.t: Ta xil rumal catit. Catecut que vaic, ma quiꜩih abixic chi qui bano; xaloc chi be iaoc qui va.
sentences.l: Then they-were-seen by their-grandmother. Then-then they eating, not truly field-work (chi) they-did-it; for-nothing(?) (chi) go given their food.
sentences.i: So their grandmother saw them. Then they ate, though they had done no real work on the field; it was for nothing (?) that their food was brought to them.
sentences.n: xil rumal catit 'they were seen by their grandmother': with rumal 'by' the verb is read as passive. que vaic 'they ate' (va 'eat', vaic 'eating', as 010). chi be iaoc qui va 'their food was brought', as chi be ya ca va in ¶12. iaoc is 'given', ya + -oc (MS iaoc, Brasseur yaoc; toggle yaoq).

sentences.t: Ta xebe cut chi cochoch: “Quiꜩih mi xoh coꜩic, ix catit,” queꜭha, que oponic.
sentences.l: Then they-went then to their-home: “Truly just-now we became-tired, you our-grandmother,” they-say, they arriving-there.
sentences.i: Then they went home. “We are truly worn out, grandmother,” they said as they came in.
sentences.n: Quiꜩih mi xoh coꜩic 'we are truly tired': xoh 'we' (completive) + coꜩ 'tire' + -ic (Brasseur 'Nous sommes véritablement fatigués'; inferred). The modern word may be kos 'tired', but the MS has the tz ligature, and the toggle respells it (kotzik). queꜭha 'they say': que 'they' (ongoing) + ꜭha 'say'. The glossary gives the same letters as 'their food'; this is a different word. que oponic 'as they arrived'.

sentences.t: Xaloc chi qui quiquih chi qui yuc puch cacan, qui ꜫab chuvach catit.
sentences.l: For-nothing(?) (chi) they stretch(?) (chi) they stretch-out(?) also their-legs, their hands before their-grandmother.
sentences.i: And for nothing (?) they stretched out (?) their legs and their arms before their grandmother.
sentences.n: qui quiquih and qui yuc are a pair. Brasseur has 'allongeant sans raison leurs jambes et leurs bras devant leur aïeule'. chi qui yuc puch is a doubtful reading: the MS has chiquaʒiuc or similar (a q-shape, a, a ʒ-like y, a u written like in). It is printed after Brasseur's yug, with the MS's plain final c. Both 'stretch' senses are guesses, and the toggle respells the letters. cacan, qui ꜫab 'their legs, their hands', a couplet for the whole body. cacan is c- 'their' + acan 'leg' (toggle kaqan), and ꜫab has the tresillo (Brasseur gab; toggle q'ab').

sentences.t: Ta xebe chicut chu caꜫih; xe opon cut pa cabix.
sentences.l: Then they-went again-then at-its-second-day; they arrived-there then in their-field.
sentences.i: The next day they went again, and came to their field.
sentences.n: chu caꜫih 'on the next day': chi + v- + ca 'second' (cab 'two') + ꜫih 'day'. The MS has chucaquih, and q + u is read ꜫ; Brasseur has chaka gih, 'le jour suivant' (inferred; toggle chu kaq'ij). pa cabix 'into their field': c- 'their' + abix, joined as written (Brasseur pa c'abix; toggle kab'ix, as 013's narrative cabix).

sentences.t: Quiz iacatahinac chic ronohel che, caam; vchapom chi rib ronohel tum, quixic, ta xe oponic.
sentences.l: All raised-up now all tree, vine; it-had-seized (chi) itself all bramble(?), thorn, when they arrived-there.
sentences.i: Everything had risen up again, all the trees and the vines, and all the brambles (?) and thorns were tangled together again, when they arrived.
sentences.n: Quiz 'completely': quiz 'finish' (toggle k'is). iacatahinac 'stood up again': yac 'lift, raise' + -atah + -inac, which marks a state already reached. The MS has iacatahinac and Brasseur vacatahinak (toggle yakatajinaq). vchapom chi rib 'had caught hold of itself', tangled: chap 'seize' + -om, which marks a finished action, with rib 'itself'. This is the second doubtful tum: the MS has tun, with only two minims, and it is printed tum, as in ¶15 (Brasseur tam). che, caam and tum, quixic are the pairs of ¶14 and ¶15.

sentences.t: “Apachinac coh michouic?” xeꜭha cut.
sentences.l: “Who us tricks(?)?” they-said then.
sentences.i: “Who is making fools (?) of us?” they said.
sentences.n: Apachinac 'who'. coh michouic: coh 'us' (k- ongoing + oh) + michou + -ic. The -ou- is the ending that names the doer, as 008's xchacou, which suits a question asking who does it. michou 'trick, make sport of' is not otherwise known, and follows Brasseur's 'Qui donc nous a ainsi joués?' (a guess; toggle michowik).

sentences.t: Are cut que banou ri ronohel chuti chicop, nima chicop: coh, balam, queh, vmul, iac, vtiu, aꜫ, ziz, chuti ꜯiquin, nima ꜯiquin; are xe banouic. Xa hun acab xqui bano.
sentences.l: This then they-did-it the all small animal, great animal: puma, jaguar, deer, rabbit, fox(?), coyote, peccary, coati(?), small bird, great bird; these they-did-it. Only one night they-did-it.
sentences.i: It was all the animals who had done it, small and great: the puma, the jaguar, the deer, the rabbit, the fox (?), the coyote, the peccary, the coati (?), the small birds and the great birds; they were the ones who did it. They did it all in a single night.
sentences.n: que banou, xe banouic 'they were the ones who did it': -ou- is the ending that names the doers, as 008's xchacou. The MS has que banou ri joined; Brasseur prints que bano u ri. chuti chicop, nima chicop … chuti ꜯiquin, nima ꜯiquin 'small animals, great animals … small birds, great birds' frame the list. The chuti before ꜯiquin is written chuh̃ in the MS, an abbreviation, expanded with Brasseur's chüti (toggle ch'uti', as earlier parts). coh 'puma' has plain c here; the animal ꜭoh of 002 was g-shaped (toggle koj, as there). balam 'jaguar'. queh 'deer', the house word. vmul 'rabbit'. iac is the modern yak, a fox or wild cat (Brasseur 'Sarigue'; inferred). vtiu 'coyote', as in Hunahpu Vtiu (001). aꜫ 'peccary, wild pig' has the tresillo (Brasseur ak, 'Sanglier'). ziz is taken as the modern sis 'coati' (Brasseur 'Porc-Epic'; inferred). xa hun acab 'in a single night': the MS clearly writes plain c, where the house word is aꜫab with the tresillo, and the toggle restores the q' (aq'ab'). The second clearing and the night watch follow in the next part.

about: Hunahpu and Xbalanque sing and play the flute and the drum, their grandmother sitting with them, and with the tune Hunahpu Coy they call back their elder brothers, now monkeys. Hunbatz and Hunchouen come dancing into the house, and the old woman, seeing their ugly faces, bursts out laughing; at once they run off to the forest. The twins allow four tries. The second time she laughs at their bellies, their tails and their chests; the third time they climb onto the house and pull faces, and she laughs again; the fourth time they do not come at all. The twins comfort her: they are here, her grandchildren, in place of their elder brothers. Hunbatz and Hunchouen were later called upon by the flute players and singers, the painters and carvers of old, but they had become animals because they were proud and mistreated their younger brothers. Then the twins begin their own work, a maize field. They set out with axe, hoe and blowgun and ask their grandmother to bring their food at noon. In the field the hoe clears the ground by itself and the axe fells the trees by itself, while the twins go hunting with the blowgun; a dove, Xmucur, is set on a stump to call when the old woman comes. When it calls they grab the tools, smear earth on their hands and wood chips on their heads, and at home they complain of being worn out. The next day the field has grown back, trees, vines, brambles and thorns. All the animals, small and great, had done it in a single night.
